title: Mock 3 · V1 · Delgado: APT and macro factor models
body:
Marco Delgado is a manager-of-managers at an investment company that uses quantitative models extensively. Delgado seeks to construct a multi-manager portfolio using some of the funds managed by portfolio managers within the firm. Lena Voss is assisting him.

Delgado uses arbitrage pricing theory (APT) as a basis for evaluating strategies and managing risks. From his earlier analysis, Voss knows that Funds A and B in Exhibit 1 are well diversified. He has not previously worked with Fund C and is puzzled by the data because it is inconsistent with APT. He asks Voss gather additional information on Fund C’s holdings and to determine if an arbitrage opportunity exists among these three investment alternatives. Her analysis, using the data in Exhibit 1, confirms that an arbitrage opportunity does exist.

Exhibit 1
Expected Returns and Factor Sensitivities (One-Factor Model)
Fund	Expected Return	Factor Sensitivity
A	0.02	0.5
B	0.05	1.5
C	0.03	0.9
Using a two-factor model, Voss now estimates the three funds’ sensitivity to inflation and GDP growth. That information is presented in Exhibit 2. Voss assumes a zero value for the error terms when working with the selected two-factor model.

Exhibit 2
Expected Returns and Factor Sensitivities (Two-Factor Model)
Fund	Expected Return	Inflation sensitivity	GDP growth sensitivity
A	0.02	0.6	0.8
B	0.05	1.6	0.0
C	0.03	1.0	1.1
Delgado asks Voss to calculate the return for Portfolio AC, composed of a 60% allocation to Fund A and 40% allocation to Fund C, using the surprises in inflation and GDP growth in Exhibit 3.

Exhibit 3
Selected Data on Factors
Factor	Research Staff Forecast	Actual Value
Inflation	1.8%	2.3%
GDP Growth	2.0%	1.2%
Finally, Delgado asks Voss about the return sensitivities of Portfolios A, B, and C given the information provided in Exhibit 3.

questions.q: Which of the following is not a key assumption of APT, which is used by Delgado to evaluate strategies and manage risks?
options: A factor model describes asset returns.
Asset-specific risk can be eliminated through diversification.
Arbitrage opportunities exist among well-diversified portfolios.
questions.why: Arbitrage pricing theory (APT) is a framework that explains the expected return of a portfolio in equilibrium as a linear function of the risk of the portfolio with respect to a set of factors capturing systematic risk. A key assumption of APT is that, in equilibrium, there are no arbitrage opportunities.

questions.q: The arbitrage opportunity identified by Voss can be exploited with:
options: Strategy 1: Buy $50,000 Fund A and $50,000 Fund B; sell short $100,000 Fund C.
Strategy 2: Buy $60,000 Fund A and $40,000 Fund B; sell short $100,000 Fund C.
Strategy 3: Sell short $60,000 of Fund A and $40,000 of Fund B; buy $100,000 Fund C.
questions.why: A portfolio of 60% Fund A and 40% Fund B has expected return 0.60 × 0.02 + 0.40 × 0.05 = 0.032, or 3.2%, and sensitivity 0.60 × 0.5 + 0.40 × 1.5 = 0.90, the same as Fund C. Fund C earns only 3.0% for the same risk, so C is overpriced relative to the mix. Buy the 60/40 mix of A and B and sell short C (Strategy 2): zero net investment, zero factor risk, riskless profit of 0.2%.

questions.q: Based on the data in Exhibit 2 and Exhibit 3, the return for Portfolio AC, given the surprises in inflation and GDP growth, is closest to:
questions.why: Surprises: inflation = 2.3% − 1.8% = +0.5%; GDP growth = 1.2% − 2.0% = −0.8%. Fund A: 2% + 0.6 × 0.5% + 0.8 × (−0.8%) = 1.66%. Fund C: 3% + 1.0 × 0.5% + 1.1 × (−0.8%) = 2.62%. Portfolio AC = 0.60 × 1.66% + 0.40 × 2.62% = 2.04%. Option A is the expected return alone (0.6 × 2% + 0.4 × 3%); option B is the surprise effect alone, without the expected returns.

questions.q: Based on the data in Exhibit 2, which fund is most sensitive to the combined surprises in inflation and GDP growth in Exhibit 3?
questions.why: Effect of the surprises on each fund: Fund A: 0.6 × 0.5% + 0.8 × (−0.8%) = -0.34%. Fund B: 1.6 × 0.5% + 0.0 × (−0.8%) = +0.80%. Fund C: 1.0 × 0.5% + 1.1 × (−0.8%) = -0.38%. Fund B has the largest combined effect in absolute size.

title: Mock 3 · V2 · Larsson: term structure of interest rates
body:
Emma Larsson is a senior bond trader for an investment bank, and Ravi Menon is a junior bond trader at the bank. Larsson is responsible for her own trading activities and also for providing assignments to Menon that will develop his skills and create profitable trade ideas. Exhibit 1 presents the current par and spot rates.

Exhibit 1
Current Par and Spot Rates
Maturity	Par Rate	Spot Rate
One year	2.00%	2.00%
Two years	2.59%	2.60%
Three years	3.08%	3.10%
Four years	3.55%	3.60%
Five years	4.05%	 
Note: Par and spot rates are based on annual-coupon sovereign bonds.
Larsson gives Menon two assignments that involve researching various questions:

Assignment 1:
What is the yield-to-maturity of the option-free, default-risk-free bond presented in Exhibit 2? Assume that the bond is held to maturity, and use the rates shown in Exhibit 1.

Exhibit 2
Selected Data for $1,000 Par Bond
Bond Name	Maturity (T)	Coupon
Bond Z	Three years	5.00%
Note: Terms are today for a T-year loan.
Assignment 2:
Assuming that the projected spot curve two years from today will be below the current forward curve, is Bond Z fairly valued, undervalued, or overvalued?

After completing his assignments, Menon asks about Larsson’s current trading activities. Larsson states that she has a two-year investment horizon and will purchase Bond Z as part of a strategy to ride the yield curve. Exhibit 1 shows Larsson’s yield curve assumptions implied by the spot rates.

questions.q: Based on Exhibit 1, the five-year spot rate is closest to:
questions.why: Forward substitution with the five-year par rate of 4.05%: price of a par bond = 1. Sum of discount factors for years 1–4 = 1/1.02 + 1/1.026² + 1/1.031³ + 1/1.036⁴ = 3.7109. Then 1 = 0.0405 × 3.7109 + 1.0405/(1+z5)⁵, so (1+z5)⁵ = 1.0405 ÷ 0.8497 = 1.2245 and z5 = 4.13%.

questions.q: Based on Exhibit 1, the forward rate of a one-year loan beginning in three years is closest to:
questions.why: f(3,1) = (1+z4)⁴ ÷ (1+z3)³ − 1 = 1.036⁴ ÷ 1.031³ − 1 = 1.1520 ÷ 1.0959 − 1 = 5.11%. Option B builds the forward from par rates instead of spot rates; option A is just the four-year spot rate.

questions.q: For Assignment 1, the yield-to-maturity for Bond Z is closest to the:
questions.why: The yield-to-maturity y3 of Bond Z is a weighted average of the spot rates used in valuation, and the largest cash flow (105) comes in year 3, so z3 gets the biggest weight. Price = 5/1.02 + 5/1.026² + 105/1.031³ = 105.46. Solving the 3-year yield on those flows gives y3 = 3.07%, closest to the three-year spot rate (3.10%).

questions.q: For Assignment 2, Menon should conclude that Bond Z is currently:
questions.why: Menon projects that the spot curve two years from today will be below the current forward curve, which implies that her expected future spot rates beyond two years will be lower than the quoted forward rates. Menon would perceive Bond Z to be undervalued in the sense that the market is effectively discounting the bond’s payments at a higher rate than she would, and the bond’s market price is below her estimate of intrinsic value.

title: Mock 3 · V3 · Pryce: Ridgeline and Prairie Oil, acquisition, synergies and capital structure
body:
Marion Pryce is an analyst at an investment bank covering the energy sector. She and her junior analyst are analyzing Ridgeline Oil Corporation.

Ridgeline Oil Corporation is a publicly traded, US-based energy company that just announced its acquisition of Prairie Oil Corporation, a smaller US-based energy company. Ridgeline will pay USD48 in cash and 1.10 Ridgeline shares for each Prairie share, for a total consideration of USD12 billion based on share prices just prior to the announcement. Ridgeline’s current trading enterprise value just prior to the announcement was USD155 billion. Pryce concludes that the acquisition does not signal a change in strategy or focus for Ridgeline.

Ridgeline expects to realize annual recurring cost synergies of USD240 million (pre-tax), primarily from efficiencies in oil exploration and production activities and savings in corporate costs. The achievement of the full USD240 million in synergies is expected by the end of the third year after the acquisition closes. Synergies are realized in the amounts of USD80 million, USD160 million, and USD240 million in Years 1–3, respectively, and cash costs of USD120 million, USD190 million, and USD270 million are incurred in Years 1–3, respectively.

Expectations for revenues and total operating expenses for Ridgeline and Prairie for the next three years prior to the acquisition announcement are shown in Exhibit 1.

Exhibit 1
Ridgeline and Prairie Year 1–3 Figures, Prior to Acquisition (USD millions)
Ridgeline	Year 1	Year 2	Year 3
Revenues	18,400	19,320	20,286
Operating expenses	14,200	14,910	15,655
Prairie			
Revenues	3,900	4,095	4,300
Operating expenses	2,350	2,470	2,590
Pryce’s junior analyst makes the following comment during a conversation with Pryce:

The acquisition is considered immaterial in the initial evaluation step for Ridgeline because it does not signal a change in strategy or focus.

Ridgeline’s offer valued Prairie at an enterprise value of USD12.6 billion, including USD1.4 billion of existing Prairie debt. To finance the consideration of USD48 in cash and 1.10 Ridgeline shares for each Prairie share, Ridgeline will issue 40 million new shares and raise approximately USD5.5 billion in new debt and fund the remainder with cash on hand. Following the close, Ridgeline expects its outstanding debt will be approximately USD36.9 billion. Prior to the acquisition, Ridgeline has 1.250 billion shares outstanding trading at USD100 per share. Pryce wants to determine how much the weights of debt and equity in Ridgeline’s capital structure will change assuming a constant share price and that the book value of debt equals its market value.

During an internal meeting, Pryce asks if Ridgeline could have achieved its same goals by undertaking an equity investment or joint venture. In response, Pryce’s junior analyst makes the following three statements.

Statement 1: Acquisitions require substantially greater capital investments than equity investments.

Statement 2: Acquisitions and equity investments are similar in that they both allow the acquirer to gain control of the target.

Statement 3: Relative to joint ventures, equity investments provide more equal governance representation and require larger investments.

Pryce conducted a sum-of-the-parts valuation of Ridgeline’s three segments and calculated an estimated enterprise value of USD150 billion just prior to the announcement.

questions.q: Based on Exhibit 1, the forecasted operating income in Year 3 for the combined Ridgeline and Prairie is closest to:
questions.why: Combined Year 3 revenues = 20,286 + 4,300 = 24,586. Combined operating expenses = 15,655 + 2,590 = 18,245. Operating income before deal effects = 24,586 − 18,245 = 6,341. Add the Year 3 synergies of 240 and subtract the Year 3 cash costs of 270: 6,341 + 240 − 270 = 6,311. Option A leaves out the synergies; option C leaves out the costs to achieve them.

questions.q: Pryce’s junior analyst’s comment about materiality is:
options: incorrect because the acquisition is considered a small acquisition.
incorrect because the acquisition represents more than 10% of Ridgeline’s enterprise value prior to the transaction.
questions.why: Materiality has two dimensions: size and fit. The acquisition does not signal a change in strategy or focus (fit is fine), and the total consideration of USD12 billion is only 12 ÷ 155 = 7.7% of Ridgeline’s enterprise value, below the 10% threshold. It is not large, so it is considered immaterial in the initial evaluation step and the comment is correct.

questions.q: The weight of equity in Ridgeline’s capital structure as a result of the acquisition of Prairie assuming Pryce’s two assumptions is closest to:
questions.why: After the close, debt = USD36.9 billion. Before the deal, Ridgeline had 36.9 − 1.4 − 5.5 = USD30.0 billion of debt and 1.250 billion × USD100 = USD125.0 billion of equity. New equity = 40 million × USD100 = USD4.0 billion, so equity after = 129.0. Weight of equity = 129.0 ÷ (129.0 + 36.9) = 77.8% ≈ 78%. Option A is the weight of debt (36.9 ÷ 165.9 = 22%); option C is the pre-deal equity weight (125.0 ÷ 155.0 = 81%).

questions.q: Ridgeline’s estimated conglomerate discount just prior to the announcement is:
questions.why: Estimated conglomerate discount = sum-of-the-parts enterprise value − current trading enterprise value = USD150 billion − USD155 billion = −USD5 billion. The sign is negative: the market values Ridgeline ABOVE the sum of its parts, so there is a premium, not a discount. (A positive figure means the market is discounting the conglomerate.)

title: Mock 3 · V4 · Sorensen: Companies A, B and C free cash flow
body:
Ingrid Sorensen manages a dividend growth strategy for a large asset management firm. Sorensen meets with her investment team to discuss potential investments in three companies: Company A, Company B, and Company C. Statements of cash flow for the three companies are presented in Exhibit 1.

Exhibit 1: Statements of Cash Flow, Most Recent Fiscal Year End (Amounts in Millions of Dollars)
	Company A	Company B	Company C
Cash Flow from Operating Activities			
Net Income	5,120	1,212	15,409
Adjustments			
  Depreciation	500	288	3,746
  Other noncash expenses	800	—	—
  Changes in working capital			
    (Increase) Decrease accounts receivable	(380)	(150)	(536)
    (Increase) Decrease inventories	—	(200)	(803)
    Increase (Decrease) accounts payable	(210)	100	(3)
    Increase (Decrease) other current liabilities	540	14	350
      Net cash from operating activities	6,370	1,264	18,163
Cash Flow from Investing Activities			
(Purchase) Sale of fixed assets	1,900	(1,000)	(3,463)
      Net cash from investing activities	1,900	(1,000)	(3,463)
Cash Flow from Financing Activities			
Increase (Decrease) notes payable	40	3000	1,238
Increase (Decrease) long-term debt	(1,200)	(1,000)	(1,379)
Payment of common stock dividends	(1,000)	(237)	(15,000)
      Net cash from financing activities	(2,160)	1,763	(15,141)
Net change in cash and cash equivalents	6,110	2,027	(441)
Cash and equivalents at beginning of year	50	100	3,000
Cash and equivalents at end of year	6,160	2,127	2,559
Supplemental Cash Flow Disclosures			
Interest	(353)	(50)	(552)
Income taxes	(1,605)	(648)	(3,787)

Sorensen’s team first discusses key characteristics of Company A. The company has a history of paying modest dividends relative to FCFE, has a stable capital structure, and is owned by a controlling investor.

The team also considers the impact of Company A’s three noncash transactions in the most recent year on its FCFE, including the following:

Transaction 1: A $700 million loss on a sale of equipment
Transaction 2: An impairment of intangibles of $450 million
Transaction 3: A $250 million reversal of a previously recorded restructuring charge

In addition, Company A’s annual report indicates that the firm expects to incur additional noncash charges related to restructuring over the next few years.

To value the three companies’ shares, one team member suggests valuing the companies’ shares using net income as a proxy for FCFE. Another team member proposes forecasting FCFE using a sales-based methodology based on the following equation:

FCFE = NI – (1 – DR)(FCInv – Dep) – (1 – DR)(WCInv).

Sorensen’s team ultimately decides to use actual free cash flow to value the three companies’ shares. Selected data and assumptions are provided in Exhibit 2.

Exhibit 2: Supplemental Data and Valuation Assumptions
	Company A	Company B	Company C
Tax rate	35%	35%	30%
Beta	1.00	0.90	1.10
Before-tax cost of debt	6%	7%	6%
Target debt ratio	50%	30%	40%
Market data:			
  Risk-free rate: 3%			
  Market risk premium: 7%			

The team calculates the intrinsic value of Company B using a two-stage FCFE model. FCFE growth rates for the first four years are estimated at 10%, 9%, 8%, and 7%, respectively, before declining to a constant 6% starting in the fifth year.

To calculate the intrinsic value of Company C’s equity, the team uses the FCFF approach assuming a single-stage model where FCFF is expected to grow at 5% indefinitely.

questions.q: Based on Company A’s key characteristics, which discounted cash flow model would most likely be used by the investment team to value Company A’s shares?
questions.why:
Three clues point to FCFE:
1. Modest dividends relative to FCFE: dividends differ a lot from the capacity to pay, so a DDM would understate value (A is wrong).
2. A controlling investor: control gives discretion over how free cash flow is used, so the owner could change the dividend policy at any time. Free cash flow models value that capacity directly.
3. A stable capital structure: FCFE values equity directly and more simply. FCFF (C) is preferred when leverage is changing or FCFE is negative, so it's needlessly indirect here.

questions.q: Which noncash transaction should be subtracted from net income in arriving at Company A’s FCFE?
questions.why: Noncash items are reversed out of net income: Transaction 1, loss on sale of equipment, reduced net income with no cash outflow → ADD back +700. Transaction 2, impairment of intangibles, reduced net income and is noncash → ADD back +450. Transaction 3, reversal of a restructuring charge, INCREASED net income with no cash inflow → SUBTRACT −250. Noncash losses and charges are added back (the first two); a noncash gain is subtracted.

questions.q: Based on Exhibit 1, Company A’s FCFE for the most recent year is closest to:
questions.why: FCFE = NI + noncash charges − WCInv − FCInv + net borrowing. Net income: 5,120. Noncash charges (depreciation 500 + other noncash 800): +1,300. Working capital investment (receivables −380, payables −210, other current liabilities +540 = −50): −50. Proceeds from sale of fixed assets: +1,900. Net borrowing (notes +40, long-term debt −1,200 = −1,160): −1,160. FCFE = $7,110 million. (Shortcut: CFO 6,370 + CFI 1,900 + net borrowing −1,160 = 7,110.) Option A leaves out the asset-sale proceeds; option B is the net change in cash, which also subtracts the 1,000 dividends.

questions.q: Based on Exhibit 1, using net income as a proxy for Company B’s FCFE would result in an intrinsic value that is:
options: lower than the intrinsic value if actual FCFE were used.
equal to the intrinsic value if actual FCFE were used.
higher than the intrinsic value if actual FCFE were used.
questions.why:
Company B's actual FCFE:
Net income: 1,212
+ Depreciation: +288
− WCInv (AR −150, inventory −200, AP +100, other CL +14 = −236): −236
− Fixed capital investment: −1,000
+ Net borrowing (notes +3,000, LT debt −1,000): +2,000
FCFE = $2,264 million
NI ($1,212m) is far BELOW FCFE ($2,264m), mainly because of the $2,000m of net borrowing, so a value built on NI is lower (B and C are wrong).
NI is only a fair proxy when depreciation ≈ capex, working capital is steady and there is no net borrowing.

title: Mock 3 · V5 · Dunn: Growth Factor Backtests and Simulations
body:
Rachel Dunn is a senior analyst for a consulting firm that specializes in assessing equity strategies using backtesting and simulation techniques. She is working with an assistant, Tyler Beck, to develop multifactor portfolio strategies based on nine factors common to the growth style of investing. To do so, Dunn and Beck plan to construct nine separate factor portfolios and then use them to create factor-weighted allocation portfolios.

Dunn tasks Beck with specifying the investment universe and determining the availability of appropriate reporting data in vendor databases. Beck selects a vendor database that does not provide point-in-time data, so he adjusts the database to include point-in-time constituent stocks and a reporting lag of four months.

Next, Dunn and Beck run initial backtests on the nine factor portfolios, calculating performance statistics and key metrics for each. For backtesting purposes, the portfolios are rebalanced monthly over a 30-year time horizon using a rolling-window procedure.

Dunn and Beck consider a variety of metrics to assess the results of the factor portfolio backtests. Dunn asks Beck what can be concluded from the data for three of the factor strategies in Exhibit 1:

Exhibit 1: Backtest Metrics for Factor Strategies
	Factor 1	Factor 2	Factor 3
VaR (95%)	(4.4%)	(1.8%)	(7.9%)
Standard deviation of returns	2.4%	1.4%	4.1%
Maximum drawdown	25.6%	9.1%	52.3%

Beck tells Dunn the following:

Statement 1: We do not need to consider maximum drawdown, because standard deviation sufficiently characterizes risk.
Statement 2: Factor 2 has the highest downside risk.

From her professional experience Dunn knows that benchmark and risk parity factor portfolios, in which factors are equally weighted and equally risk weighted, respectively, are popular with institutional and high-net-worth clients. To gain a more complete picture of these investment strategies’ performance, Dunn and Beck design a Benchmark Portfolio (A) and a Risk Parity Portfolio (B), and then run two simulation methods to generate investment performance data based on the underlying factor portfolios, assuming 1,000 simulation trials for each approach:

Approach 1: Historical simulation
Approach 2: Monte Carlo simulation

Dunn and Beck discuss the differences between the two approaches and then design the simulations, making key decisions at various steps. During the process, Dunn expresses a number of concerns:

Concern 1: Returns from six of the nine factors are correlated.
Concern 2: The distribution of Factor 1 returns exhibits excess kurtosis and negative skewness.
Concern 3: The number of simulations needed for Approach 1 is larger than the size of the historical dataset.

For each approach, Dunn and Beck run 1,000 trials to obtain 1,000 returns for Portfolios A and B. To help understand the effect of the skewness and excess kurtosis observed in the Factor 1 returns on the performance of Portfolios A and B, Beck suggests simulating an additional 1,000 factor returns using a multivariate skewed Student’s t-distribution, then repeating the Approach 2 simulation.

questions.q: Following Beck’s adjustments to the initial vendor database, backtested returns will most likely be subject to:
questions.why:
A four-month (≈120-day) reporting lag removes look-ahead bias, but it's longer than needed: many large companies report within 30–50 days of quarter end. So the backtest often uses figures that are older than what investors actually had, which is STALE data.
B and C are wrong: data snooping and p-hacking are the same problem, a flawed process of searching the data until something looks significant. They're about how the researcher behaves, not a feature that adjusting a database can add.

questions.q: Based on Exhibit 1, Beck should conclude that:
options: Factor Strategy 3 has the highest portfolio turnover.
Factor Strategy 2 has less downside risk than Strategy 3.
Factor Strategy 2 has the highest returns.
questions.why: VaR and maximum drawdown are both DOWNSIDE risk measures. Factor 2: VaR 1.8%, maximum drawdown 9.1%. Factor 3: VaR 7.9%, maximum drawdown 52.3%. Factor 2 is lower on both, so it has less downside risk than Factor 3. Exhibit 1 says nothing about turnover, and it shows only risk measures, not returns.

questions.q: Which of Beck’s statements about Exhibit 1 is incorrect?
questions.why: Statement 1 is incorrect: standard deviation measures VOLATILITY (both directions); maximum drawdown measures DOWNSIDE risk (the worst cumulative loss from peak to trough). They may be correlated, but one does not replace the other, especially with fat-tailed, skewed returns. Statement 2 is incorrect: Factor 2 has the LOWEST VaR (1.8%) and lowest maximum drawdown (9.1%), so it has the LOWEST downside risk, not the highest.

questions.q: To address Concern 3 when designing Approach 1, Dunn should:
options: add monthly return observations to the dataset using interpolation.
randomly sample from the historical returns with replacement.
choose the multivariate normal distribution as the initial functional form.
questions.why:
When more trials are needed than there are historical observations, sample WITH replacement (bootstrapping). Each draw comes from the same full dataset, with equal probability (uniform draw), so 1,000 trials can come from fewer data points.
A is wrong: interpolation invents returns that never happened, which goes against the point of historical simulation.
C is wrong: choosing a distribution is a Monte Carlo step, and it doesn't fix the shortage of historical data.

title: Mock 3 · V6 · Ashby: Harrowgate PLC and Telford
body:
Colin Ashby, CFA, is an equity analyst with a UK-based investment firm. One firm Ashby follows is Harrowgate PLC, a UK-based company. On 31 December 2018, Harrowgate paid £360 million to purchase a 50 percent stake in Telford Company. The excess of the purchase price over the fair value of Telford’s net assets was attributable to previously unrecorded licenses. These licenses were estimated to have an economic life of seven years. The fair value of Telford’s assets and liabilities other than licenses was equal to their recorded book values. Harrowgate and Telford both use the pound sterling as their reporting currency and prepare their financial statements in accordance with IFRS.

Ashby is concerned whether the investment should affect his “buy” rating on Harrowgate common stock. He knows Harrowgate could choose one of several accounting methods to report the results of its investment, but Harrowgate has not announced which method it will use. Ashby forecasts that both companies’ 2019 financial results (excluding any merger accounting adjustments) will be identical to those of 2018.

Harrowgate’s and Telford’s condensed income statements for the year ended 31 December 2018, and condensed balance sheets at 31 December 2018, are presented in Exhibits 1 and 2, respectively.

Exhibit 1: Harrowgate PLC and Telford Company Income Statements for the Year Ended 31 December 2018 (£ millions)
	Harrowgate	Telford
Net sales	950	510
Cost of goods sold	(495)	(305)
Selling expenses	(50)	(15)
Administrative expenses	(136)	(49)
Depreciation & amortization expense	(102)	(92)
Interest expense	(42)	(32)
Income before taxes	125	17
Income tax expense	(50)	(7)
Net income	75	10

Exhibit 2: Harrowgate PLC and Telford Company Balance Sheets at 31 December 2018 (£ millions)
	Harrowgate	Telford
Cash	50	20
Receivables—net	70	45
Inventory	130	75
Total current assets	250	140
Property, plant, & equipment—net	1,570	930
Investment in Telford	360	—
Total assets	2,180	1,070
Current liabilities	110	90
Long-term debt	600	400
Total liabilities	710	490
Common stock	890	535
Retained earnings	580	45
Total equity	1,470	580
Total liabilities and equity	2,180	1,070
Note: Balance sheets reflect the purchase price paid by Harrowgate, but do not yet consider the impact of the accounting method choice.

questions.q: Harrowgate’s current ratio on 31 December 2018 most likely will be highest if the results of the acquisition are reported using:
questions.why:
Equity method: the investment is one non-current line, so only Harrowgate's own current items count:
250 ÷ 110 = 2.27
Consolidation (full OR partial goodwill) adds 100% of Telford's current assets and liabilities:
250 + 140 ÷ 110 + 90 = 390 ÷ 200 = 1.95
Telford's own current ratio (140/90 = 1.56) is lower than Harrowgate's, so adding it drags the ratio down. B and C give the same 1.95; goodwill doesn't touch current items.

questions.q: Harrowgate’s long-term debt to equity ratio on 31 December 2018 most likely will be lowest if the results of the acquisition are reported using:
questions.why: Equity method: 600 ÷ 1,470 = 0.41 (Telford’s debt stays off Harrowgate’s balance sheet). Consolidation: debt = 600 + 400 = 1,000; equity = 1,470 + 360 non-controlling interest (NCI) = 1,830; 1,000 ÷ 1,830 = 0.55. Full vs partial goodwill makes no difference: the whole excess went to licenses, so goodwill is zero and NCI is £360m either way (50% × £720m fair value of net assets).

questions.q: Based on Ashby’s forecast, if Harrowgate deems it has acquired control of Telford, Harrowgate’s consolidated 2019 depreciation and amortization expense (in £ millions) will be closest to:
questions.why: Step 1 – value the licenses: implied fair value of 100% of Telford = 360 ÷ 0.50 = £720m. Book (= fair) value of recorded net assets = £580m → licenses = 720 − 580 = £140m. Step 2 – amortize over 7 years: 140 ÷ 7 = £20m a year. Step 3 – consolidate 100% of both companies: 102 + 92 + 20 = £214m. A (102) is Harrowgate alone (equity-method view). B (148) adds only 50% of Telford’s D&A (102 + 46), like proportionate consolidation, and ignores the license amortization.

questions.q: Based on Ashby’s forecast, Harrowgate’s net profit margin for 2019 most likely will be highest if the results of the acquisition are reported using:
questions.why: Net income to Harrowgate’s shareholders is the SAME under every method: 75 + 50% × 10 − 50% × 20 = 75 + 5 − 10 = £70m. Sales differ: the equity method shows only £950m; consolidation shows 950 + 510 = £1,460m. Same profit ÷ smaller sales = higher margin under the equity method (70 ÷ 950 = 7.4% vs 70 ÷ 1,460 = 4.8%).

title: Mock 3 · V7 · Reinholt: Orion Credit Analysis
body:
Sofia Reinholt is a senior bond analyst at Orion Investment Management. Mara Kessel, a junior analyst, works for Reinholt in helping conduct fixed-income research for the firm’s portfolio managers. Reinholt and Kessel meet to discuss several bond positions held in the firm’s portfolios.

Bonds I and II both have a maturity of one year, an annual coupon rate of 6%, and a market price equal to par value. The risk-free rate is 3.5%. Historical default experiences of bonds comparable to Bonds I and II are presented in Exhibit 1.

Exhibit 1: Credit Risk Information for Comparable Bonds
Bond	Recovery Rate	Percentage of Bonds That Survive and Make Full Payment
I	45%	97%
II	30%	98.5%

Bond III is a zero-coupon bond with three years to maturity. Reinholt evaluates similar bonds and estimates a recovery rate of 40% and a risk-neutral default probability of 1.5%, assuming conditional probabilities of default. Kessel creates Exhibit 2 to compute Bond III’s credit valuation adjustment. She assumes a flat yield curve at 3.5%, with exposure, recovery, and loss given default values expressed per 100 of par value.

Exhibit 2: Analysis of Bond III
Date	Exposure	Recovery	Loss Given Default	Probability of Default	Probability of Survival	Expected Loss	Present Value of Expected Loss
0							
1	93.3511	37.3404	56.0106	1.5000%	98.5000%	0.8402	0.8117
2	96.6184	38.6473	57.9710	1.4775%	97.0225%	0.8565	0.7996
3	100.0000	40.0000	60.0000	1.4553%	95.5672%	0.8732	0.7876
Sum				4.4328%		2.5699	2.3989

Bond IV is an AA rated bond that matures in six years, has a coupon rate of 5.5%, and a modified duration of 3.8. Reinholt is concerned about whether this bond will be downgraded to an A rating, but she does not expect the bond to default during the next year. Kessel constructs a partial transition matrix, which is presented in Exhibit 3, and suggests using a model to predict the rating change of Bond IV using leverage ratios, return on assets, and macroeconomic variables.

Exhibit 3: Partial One-Year Corporate Transition Matrix (entries in %)
From/To	AAA	AA	A
AAA	92.00	6.00	1.00
AA	3.00	87.00	9.00
A	0.05	1.00	85.00
Credit Spread (%)	0.60	1.10	2.05

Kessel calculates the risk-neutral probabilities, compares them with the actual default probabilities of bonds evaluated over the past 10 years, and observes that the actual and risk-neutral probabilities differ. She makes two observations regarding the comparison of these probabilities:

Observation 1: Actual default probabilities include the default risk premium associated with the uncertainty in the timing of the possible default loss.
Observation 2: The observed spread over the yield on a risk-free bond in practice includes liquidity and tax considerations, in addition to credit risk.

questions.q: Based on Exhibit 1, the expected future value of Bond I at maturity is closest to:
questions.why: No default (97%): receive 106. Default (3%): receive recovery = 106 × 0.45 = 47.70. Expected value = 0.97 × 106 + 0.03 × 47.70 = 102.82 + 1.43 = 104.25. Option B leaves out the coupon (0.97 × 100 + 0.03 × 45 = 97.00 + 1.35 = 98.35); option C is the payoff only if there is no default.

questions.q: Based on Exhibit 1, the risk-neutral default probability for Bond I is closest to:
questions.why: Set the price equal to the expected payoff under the risk-neutral probability P*, discounted at the risk-free rate: 100 = [106 × (1 − P*) + 47.70 × P*] ÷ 1.035. So 103.5 = 106 − 58.3 P*, P* = 2.5 ÷ 58.3 = 4.288%. Option B is the ACTUAL historical default rate (1 − 97%); option C puts the 3.5 interest in the numerator instead of the 2.5 net gain (3.5 ÷ 58.3).

questions.q: Based on Exhibit 2, the credit valuation adjustment for Bond III is closest to:
questions.why: CVA = sum of the PRESENT VALUES of expected losses = 0.8117 + 0.7996 + 0.7876 = 2.3989 (per 100 of par). Option C is the undiscounted sum of expected losses; option A is the sum of the default probabilities.

questions.q: Based on Exhibit 3, if Bond IV’s credit rating changes during the next year to an A rating, its expected price change would be closest to:
questions.why: %ΔP ≈ −ModDur × Δspread. Spread change AA → A = 2.05% − 1.10% = 0.95%. %ΔP = −3.8 × 0.0095 = −3.61%. Option A is the PROBABILITY of an AA → A migration (9%), not a price change; option C uses the whole A spread (−3.8 × 2.05%) instead of the change.

title: Mock 3 · V8 · Hale: Pacific Rim Advisory Partners
body:
Nora Hale, CFA, is currently working as a capital market adviser in a developing country. While attending a regional securities exchange conference, she introduces herself to Victor Lam, CFA. Lam is one of several partners at Pacific Rim Advisory Partners, a consulting firm specializing in capital market expansion in developing countries. When making her introduction, Hale states, “I’m an independent adviser working with the government of a developing country to improve its capital market sector. I’ve heard a lot about the work you’ve done. Could we talk about my consulting assignment and a possible role for you?”

Hale continues, “I’m looking for someone with your background and stellar reputation to help create a strategic plan to develop the asset management industry. The client’s goal is to get the Securities Exchange to be a part of a regional exchange. This will help the locally listed companies gain more exposure. However, given the budget I’ve been given, I can afford to hire only an individual. Lam, would this be of interest to you?”

Hale continues the conversation by informing Lam that she will also be approaching other industry participants, particularly in the fund management industry, who are attending the conference. Lam responds, “I sure hope you are not talking to Oscar Pell, who manages several startup funds. I think he has a drinking problem. There is a rumor his last startup fund was not well received by the investors, likely due to his drinking. As one charterholder to another, please do your due diligence first before you hire anyone. As you have already pointed out, my reputation is stellar. Why don’t we meet tonight for dinner at my ‘members only’ club to discuss your project further? I can introduce you to other influential people who are currently looking for experienced advisers in your field for upcoming assignments. I’m sure if they knew we were working together, it would really go a long way in obtaining future assignments from these industry leaders.”

Hale informs Lam that she is unfortunately not able to meet him for dinner because of a previous engagement. She subsequently says to Lam, “I’m wondering how you would respond to a situation whereby a regulator chooses not to implement extensive policies and regulations regarding the integrity of capital markets I recommended. They say my suggested policies and regulations related to market manipulation, material nonpublic information, and protecting client interests are too complicated, and they do not have the judicial competency to back them up. Consequently, they have requested I recommend just one primary rule.” Thereafter, Hale seeks out Oscar Pell, a CFA candidate, to ask for his version of what happened with his investors. Pell responds, “What actually happened was I got sick in a restaurant after having an adverse reaction to some medication. People uploaded photos to social media and stated I was falling over drunk. Subsequently, I wrote a letter to the investors explaining the situation and assuring them I had found another highly qualified fund manager after several weeks to take over until such time I had fully recovered. When I could, I looked at the fund when I was in the hospital for a week, but the fund needs close supervision, so that’s why I wanted to find another manager. One investor commented, ‘Key-person risk was not identified in the fund’s prospectus.’ Within one week we sent out a revision to the prospectus identifying key-person risk.”

questions.q: To avoid violating any CFA Institute Standards of Professional Conduct, which of the following is Lam’s most appropriate response to Hale’s question?
options: “I will need to touch base with my partners.”
“I’m not able to take on projects as an individual.”
“I can refer you to another independent adviser.”
questions.why: Standard IV, Duties to Employers: the work is a business opportunity for Lam's firm. Taking it as an individual would compete with his firm and deprive it of his skills and revenue (IV(A) Loyalty) and mean extra pay from a competing activity (IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements). He should first take it to his partners, who might, for example, cut their fees to win it. B shuts the firm out without asking. C hands the opportunity to someone else, again without giving his firm the chance.

questions.q: In the continued conversation between Hale and Lam, which sub-standard of Standard I: Professionalism did Lam least likely violate?
questions.why: I(C) Misrepresentation is least likely violated: Hale herself called his reputation stellar, so repeating it is not a misrepresentation. A is violated: I(D) Misconduct (labelled I(A) in your source): spreading a rumour that Pell drinks damages another's reputation and reflects badly on Lam's integrity. C is violated: I(B), hinting that influential contacts would give Hale future work if she hires him is a benefit meant to sway her choice of adviser.

questions.q: Which of the following should Lam most likely advise with regard to the regulator’s request?
options: Ban the “pumping up” of investment prices
Require material information be made public within 24 hours
When trading, insist service providers give preference to investors
questions.why: One broad rule that puts investors' interests first covers the most ground: it supports loyalty to clients and also makes trading on material nonpublic information and market manipulation unacceptable, since both put others ahead of investors. A is too narrow: it targets only information-based manipulation, not transaction-based manipulation or insider trading. B could harm investors: not all material information should be public (e.g. competitive secrets).

questions.q: During the conversation between Pell and Hale, Pell revealed he had most likely violated which CFA Institute Standards of Professional Conduct?
options: Standard V: Investment Analysis, Recommendations, and Actions
Both Standard I: Professionalism and Standard V: Investment Analysis, Recommendations, and Actions
questions.why: Pell was effectively the fund's only manager, yet key-person risk was missing from the prospectus. That omission is a misrepresentation under I(C) (Standard I), and failing to disclose a significant risk of the investment process breaches V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients (Standard V). So both Standards were violated, even though he later corrected the prospectus.

title: Mock 3 · V9 · Sutter: Company QRS Bank Analysis
body:
Monica Sutter is a financial sector analyst writing an industry report. In the report, Sutter discusses the relative global systemic risk across industries, referencing Industry A (international property and casualty insurance), Industry B (credit unions), and Industry C (global commercial banks).

Part of Sutter’s analysis focuses on Company QRS, a global commercial bank, and its CAMELS rating, risk management practices, and performance. First, Sutter considers the firm’s capital adequacy as measured by the key capital ratios (common equity Tier 1 capital, total Tier 1 capital, and total capital) in Exhibit 1.

Exhibit 1: Company QRS: Excerpt from Annual Report Disclosure
At 31 December	2017 $m	2016 $m	2015 $m
Regulatory capital			
   Common equity Tier 1 capital	150,200	143,000	136,500
   Additional Tier 1 capital	21,000	20,000	18,000
   Tier 2 capital	27,000	26,000	25,000
   Total regulatory capital	198,200	189,000	179,500
Risk-weighted assets (RWAs) by risk type			
   Credit risk	980,000	975,000	960,000
   Market risk	40,000	38,000	45,000
   Operational risk	280,000	270,000	230,000
Total RWAs	1,300,000	1,283,000	1,235,000

To assess Company QRS’s risk management practices, Sutter reviews the loan loss analysis in Exhibit 2.

Exhibit 2: Company QRS: Loan Loss Analysis Data
At 31 December	2017 $m	2016 $m	2015 $m
Consumer loans			
   Allowance for loan losses	11,700	12,400	12,500
   Provision for loan losses	1,800	2,600	3,300
   Charge-offs	3,650	3,800	4,000
   Recoveries	1,150	1,100	1,100
   Net charge-offs	2,500	2,700	2,900
Commercial loans			
   Allowance for loan losses	1,300	850	500
   Provision for loan losses	800	650	400
   Charge-offs	950	800	700
   Recoveries	600	500	500
   Net charge-offs	350	300	200

Finally, Sutter notes the following supplementary information from Company QRS’s annual report:

• Competition in the commercial loan space has become increasingly fierce, leading QRS managers to pursue higher-risk strategies to increase market share.
• The net benefit plan obligation has steadily decreased during the last three years.
• Company QRS awards above-average equity-based compensation to its top managers.

questions.q: Which of the following industries most likely has the highest level of global systemic risk?
questions.why:
Global commercial banks (C) have the largest share of CROSS-BORDER business and the widest network of links to other institutions, so a failure spreads furthest.
A (international P&C insurers): less cross-border business; foreign branches usually must hold local assets to cover local policy liabilities, and many insured events (autos, homes) have only local impact.
B (credit unions): member-owned, local depository institutions, with the LOWEST global systemic risk.

questions.q: Based on Exhibit 1, Company QRS’s capital adequacy over the last three years, as measured by the three key capital ratios, signals conditions that are:
Based on Exhibit 2, a loan loss analysis for the last three years indicates that:
options: the cushion between the allowance and the net commercial loan charge-offs has declined.
Company QRS has become less conservative in its provisioning for consumer loans.
the provision for commercial loan losses has trailed the actual net charge-off experience.
questions.why: Figures for 2015 → 2016 → 2017. Consumer provision ÷ net charge-offs: 3,300 ÷ 2,900 = 1.14 → 2,600 ÷ 2,700 = 0.96 → 1,800 ÷ 2,500 = 0.72. The provision has fallen below net charge-offs, so QRS has become LESS conservative in provisioning for consumer loans. Commercial provision ÷ net charge-offs: 400 ÷ 200 = 2.00 → 650 ÷ 300 = 2.17 → 800 ÷ 350 = 2.29 (provision stays above charge-offs, so it has not trailed them). Commercial allowance ÷ net charge-offs: 500 ÷ 200 = 2.50 → 850 ÷ 300 = 2.83 → 1,300 ÷ 350 = 3.71 (the cushion has risen, not declined).

questions.q: Which of the following supplemental factors is consistent with a favorable assessment of Company QRS’s financial outlook?
questions.why:
A steadily DECREASING net benefit plan obligation means less risk from the pension plan → favorable.
A is unfavorable: fierce competition is pushing managers into higher-risk strategies to win market share.
C is unfavorable: above-average equity-based pay can encourage managers to take excessive risk to lift the share price.

title: Mock 3 · V10 · Ortega: Beacon & Hart Partners
body:
Elena Ortega, CFA, is the chief compliance officer for Beacon & Hart Partners (B&H), a midsize investment management firm managing equities. B&H recently terminated Anders Keane, CFA, for multiple violations of firm policies that included violations of the Standards. Ortega composed an email to file a complaint against Keane with the Professional Conduct Program (PCP) of CFA Institute. Her email outlines Keane’s actions with three points:

Point 1

Keane was an assistant trader and worked closely with the firm’s head trader. Together, they executed trades for the firm’s equity portfolios that ranged across the market capitalization spectrum. Keane specialized in executing trades for the firm’s small-cap products and was instrumental in implementing several technology-based trading platforms. He was excited about his position and often talked with his cousin Dana Whitfield about his job as well as the companies being researched and trades being executed. B&H has a company policy to prohibit their employees from discussing trades they are executing.

Point 2

Keane was often involved in new client presentations to explain the different trading technologies utilized by the trading department. During such a meeting, a potential client talked about using a directed brokerage arrangement. They explained they had not yet decided on a broker and asked if the traders had any recommendation. Keane talked about the advantages and disadvantages of such an arrangement and mentioned how several of B&H’s clients used Sterling & Sterling (S&S). He also talked about how S&S was committed to professional development, and they had sponsored his full attendance at a three-day conference held at an exclusive winter resort.

Point 3

Another incident was discovered by one of our portfolio managers who is a member of a large online investment club. The manager noticed a new member of the group continually talked about the small-cap stocks B&H was actively trading and his arguments went against the firm’s recommendations. The manager notified me, and after several weeks of investigation, we determined that Keane was the individual discussing the companies the firm was trading. After outlining this last item, Ortega drafted the following polices to prevent and detect this type of violation going forward:

Policy 1: Membership in online investment clubs is permissible but must be reported to the Compliance Department before joining.

Policy 2: When it is discovered that a membership has not been reported, increase supervision on the employee who failed to report.

Policy 3: Send periodic reminders regarding investment club membership to those employees who failed to report and outline permissible conduct.

Ortega completed the email and sent it as well as the evidence she had gathered to the appropriate email address at the CFA Institute. She then met with B&H’s CEO to update him about the complaint and discuss what she should do next. He made the following recommendations:

Recommendation 1: Consult with the firm’s securities attorney.

Recommendation 2: Wait for the PCP to provide her with additional information.

Recommendation 3: Inform the local CFA Society about the complaint.

questions.q: As described in point 1 of the email, which Standard has Keane least likely violated?
questions.why: Standard VI(B), Priority of Transactions, is about trades in accounts where the member is a beneficial owner coming after client trades. Keane only talked to his cousin; there is no evidence he traded or had a beneficial interest in any account, so VI(B) is not engaged. A is violated: IV(A) Loyalty forbids divulging the employer's confidential information (and B&H prohibits discussing trades). C is violated: III(E) requires keeping information about clients' trades confidential.

questions.q: As described in point 2 of the email, are Keane's actions in the presentation for a new client consistent with the Standards?
options: No, his actions are inconsistent with the Standard relating to disclosure of conflicts
No, his actions are inconsistent with the Standard relating to independence and objectivity
questions.why: Standard I(B), Independence and Objectivity: accepting a broker's sponsorship of a full three-day conference at an exclusive resort is a lavish benefit that could reasonably compromise his objectivity, and he then pointed a prospective client toward that broker. Modest gifts are fine; this is not. B is wrong: he openly mentioned S&S's sponsorship, so he did not hide the conflict (VI(A)). Disclosure does not cure accepting a benefit that compromises independence.

questions.q: In point 3 of the email, which of the policies Ortega drafted is most likely insufficient to prevent a violation of the Standards?
questions.why: Standard IV(C), Responsibilities of Supervisors: periodic reminders of compliance procedures and of permissible conduct should go to ALL relevant employees, not only those who already failed to report. Policy 3 is too narrow. Policy 1 (report club membership before joining) helps prevent and detect problems, and Policy 2 (increase supervision of someone who broke the rule) matches the guidance to tighten supervision once a violation is found.

questions.q: Which of the CEO’s recommendations regarding what Ortega should do next is her best course of action to be consistent with the Standards?
questions.why: Standard I(A), Knowledge of the Law: the firm has already dissociated from Keane by firing him. The Code doesn't require reporting to regulators unless the law does, but it can be prudent, so consulting legal and compliance advisers is the right next step. B is wrong: once a complaint is filed, the matter is between Keane and CFA Institute; the PCP won't report back to her. C is wrong: telling the local CFA society could breach the confidentiality of the PCP process.

title: Mock 3 · V11 · Rao: FX trading desk, forward premium and arbitrage
body:
Sanjay Rao is an analyst at an investment bank’s foreign exchange trading desk. He meets with two of his clients to discuss their currency-related transactions.

Cairns Technologies

Cairns Technologies is an Australia-based multinational company with subsidiaries in Tokyo and London. Cairns will receive a cash inflow denominated in JPY from the Tokyo subsidiary and wants to convert this JPY receipt into Australian dollars (AUD). Rao collects the spot rate bid/offer quotes for JPY/AUD (number of JPY per AUD) in Exhibit 1. Rao investigates whether a triangular arbitrage opportunity exists between the Interbank and dealer quotes in the JPY/AUD. 

Exhibit 1 Spot Exchange Rate Bid/Offer Quotes
Interbank quote JPY/USD	104.10/104.12
Interbank quote USD/AUD	0.7480/0.7484
Dealer quote JPY/AUD	77.95/77.99
The Australian office expects a GBP cash inflow in six months from the London subsidiary. Rao collects the AUD/GBP exchange rate and interest rate information in Exhibit 2 and assumes that covered interest rate parity holds. 

Exhibit 2 AUD/GBP Spot Exchange Rate and Interest Rates
Current spot rate (AUD/GBP)	1.9240
6-month reference rate (AUD)	2.4%
6-month reference rate (GBP)	0.8%
The Fremantle Fund

The Fremantle Fund is an investment fund based in Australia. One year ago, Fremantle entered a carry trade involving currency positions in Country D and Country E. Rao calculates the all‑in return from the carry trade using the information in Exhibit 3. 

Exhibit 3 Data for Calculating Return on Carry Trade
Spot rate for currency E per currency D one year ago	7.2100
Current spot rate for currency E per currency D	7.3400
Annual yield on currency D one year ago	0.40%
Annual yield on currency E one year ago	3.60%
Fremantle wants to expand its investments into emerging markets and Rao conducts further analysis. Country A is an emerging market, has a floating-rate currency regime and highly mobile foreign capital flows. The government is rapidly increasing its fiscal stimulus to boost economic growth. Rao believes that this will lead to a prolonged buildup in public debt, which foreign creditors eventually will not accept. To ease concerns regarding the buildup in public debt, the central bank is implementing a restrictive monetary policy. He assesses the potential effect on the country’s currency based on the Mundell-Fleming and portfolio balance approaches.

questions.q: Based on Exhibit 1, does a triangular arbitrage opportunity exist in JPY/AUD?
options: Yes, by buying AUD in the interbank market and selling it to the dealer.
Yes, by buying AUD from the dealer and selling it in the interbank market.
questions.why: Implied interbank JPY/AUD bid = 104.10 × 0.7480 = 77.87; implied offer = 104.12 × 0.7484 = 77.92. Interbank cross-rate = 77.87/77.92. The dealer’s bid (77.95) is ABOVE the interbank implied offer (77.92), so buy AUD in the interbank market at 77.92 JPY and sell it to the dealer at 77.95 JPY: a riskless profit of about 0.03 JPY per AUD. Triangular arbitrage exists.

questions.q: Based on Exhibit 2, the 6-month forward rate for AUD/GBP should trade closest to a:
options: premium of 0.0153 to the spot rate.
discount of 0.0153 to the spot rate.
premium of 0.0308 to the spot rate.
questions.why: GBP is the base currency in AUD/GBP, so the higher-interest-rate currency (AUD, the price currency) trades at a forward premium. F = S × (1 + r_AUD × 0.5) ÷ (1 + r_GBP × 0.5) = 1.9240 × 1.012 ÷ 1.004 = 1.9393. Forward premium = 1.9393 − 1.9240 = 0.0153. Option B treats AUD as the base currency (wrong sign); option C forgets the six-month scaling (1.9240 × 0.016 = 0.0308).

questions.q: Based on Exhibit 3, the all-in return (in currency D terms) on Fremantle’s carry trade is closest to:
questions.why: Borrow currency D (cheap, 0.40%), invest in currency E (3.60%). Per 1 D: 7.2100 E invested grows to 7.2100 × 1.036 = 7.4696 E; convert at 7.3400 E per D = 1.0177 D. Repay the loan: 1.0040 D. All-in return = 1.0177 − 1.0040 = 1.37%. Option B is just the yield gap (3.60% − 0.40%), ignoring the currency move; option A ignores the funding cost.

questions.q: Based on Rao’s observations and the Mundell-Fleming and portfolio balance approaches, Country A’s currency would be expected to:
options: appreciate in the short term but depreciate in the long term.
depreciate in the short term towards a lower, long-term equilibrium exchange rate.
appreciate in the short term towards a higher, long-term equilibrium exchange rate.
questions.why: because the Mundell-Fleming model is a short-term model while the portfolio balance channel looks at long-term fiscal effects. In the short term the Mundell-Fleming model indicates that a more expansionary fiscal policy should cause the currency to appreciate (given highly mobile capital conditions and a restrictive monetary policy). But over the longer term the portfolio balance channel would indicate that as foreign holdings of bonds issued by the balance of trade deficit country increase, these foreign bondholders may wish to reduce their portfolio weights in that country and sell its currency. | B. Incorrect because in the shorter-term the currency is more likely to appreciate (Mundell-Fleming model) than depreciate. | C. Incorrect because although there may be short-term currency appreciation, longer-term fiscal effects are likely to cause depreciation.
